item.title: From India's Fields to Global Credits: Why We Backed Prithu
item.description: Transition VC invested ₹10 Cr in Prithu’s seed round.
item.dc:creator: Manasvi Patel
item.content:encoded:
In Part 1, we argued that carbon markets are not broken - they are recalibrating around trust.
In Part 2, we extended that idea further: markets only scale when they behave like infrastructure, not fragmented transactions.

This is where regenerative agriculture becomes critical. Regenerative agriculture is one of the few nature-based pathways that can scale meaningful carbon removal with established science and visible demand.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

In India, this is a systems problem - fragmented landholdings, weak baseline data, and high verification costs make most projects either small or unreliable, resulting in a structural gap: credible supply remains scarce even as demand consolidates around high-integrity, nature-based credits.

We invested in Prithu because they are solving this problem where it exists - on the ground.

Regen Ag’s Scale Challenge

Regenerative agriculture holds unique promise for India: 7-9 million hectares already transitioning, with practices like reduced tillage, cover cropping, and agroforestry sequestering 2-4 tCO2e per hectare annually. Yet scaling remains elusive. Over 85% of farmers hold under 2 hectares, creating coordination challenges for monitoring, compliance, and baselines in variable microclimates.

This positions Prithu in a structurally scarce supply segment - credible nature-based credits - amid global demand shifting to 500-700 MtCO2e post-2027, driven by CORSIA and Article 6. India’s organic-transitioning land alone could yield 2-4 tCO2e/ha/year, but execution gaps leave most untapped.

Most projects either cut corners for speed or stay rigorous but small. Prithu rejects that trade-off, prioritizing execution in this unstructured reality.

Field Execution as Foundation

Prithu starts with farmer aggregation via localized field representatives managing 400-500 farmers each. Onboarding takes 10-20 minutes with geo-tagged records, with a fully loaded onboarding cost ~10x below industry benchmarks.

This enables ongoing engagement: practices are observed, reinforced, and adjusted, not assumed post-onboard. Deviations surface early, keeping data dynamic and audit-ready. In a market where field behaviour drives verification, this layer ensures reliability.

Execution is the moat - ~10x lower onboarding cost, 400-500 farmers per agent, and near-zero attrition signal capital efficiency that turns pilots into scale. This density de-risks issuance (90-95% odds post-registration) and creates compounding year-on-year cashflows per hectare.

GTM Built for Farmers

Prithu’s go-to-market centers farmers: 40% revenue share via direct benefit transfers, performance incentives for reps, and ties to FPOs for trust. Near-zero attrition reflects clear economics and sustained support.

It’s vertical control from origination to sale, across 43,000 hectares onboarded - this density turns fragmented land into scalable projects.

Farmer-first GTM aligns incentives and leverages district-level access for rapid ramp -43k ha live, 5 lakh ha coming up. This operational reality outperforms partner-led peers, ensuring predictable monetization.

MRV in Service of Execution

Prithu’s digital MRV supports this: geo-tagged field proofs, satellite validation, and hashed trails compress timelines and boost issuance odds to 90-95% post-registration. It’s hybrid by design - tech aids redundancy, but field oversight remains core. We see strength in operations, not tech as the primary edge.

Once registered (12-15 months), projects yield credits for 25-30 years at falling costs, creating long-duration assets.

Hybrid DMRV targets trust deficits - field proof-of-work plus satellite checks yield audit-ready data, moving from estimates to verifiable performance, assuring premiums without over-relying on unproven data.

Durable Expansion, Regen Core

Regen-ag drives volume; biochar partnerships add permanence, capital-light, leveraging existing networks for soil application and verification.

Diversification balances volume with upside of cashflow, mitigating risks, and preserves ROIC as the platform scales to its cumulative potential.

Carbon markets scale when reliable enough to underwrite here, in India’s complexity. Prithu builds that system through farmer focus and execution, proving that if it works amid fragmentation, it works anywhere.

India’s chaos is climate tech’s proving ground. Prithu is building credible supply here, redefining markets - one farmer cluster at a time.

item.title: The Missing Layer in Carbon Markets: Verifiable Supply
item.description: Part 2 of 2: Why carbon markets only scale when they become underwriteable, and why India will decide whether that happens.
item.dc:creator: Manasvi Patel
item.content:encoded:
In Part 1, we argued that carbon markets have a trust problem, not a demand problem. Buyers are still here. What they are no longer willing to do is buy credits whose integrity depends on fragile baselines, indirect measurement, and assumptions that cannot withstand scrutiny.

Part 2 asks the harder question: what does it take to build a market that can scale, and deserves capital.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

What A Functional Carbon Market Requires

If measurement improves, baselines standardise, and risk is priced explicitly, carbon credits stop behaving like fragile instruments and start behaving like infrastructure.

That shift is not semantic. It changes who participates, how capital flows, and what scale becomes possible. Today, transactions are episodic - short-term, inconsistent, and fragmented. The market clears, but it doesn’t compound.

A high-integrity system changes that.

First, credits become underwriteable.
When measurement is continuous, and uncertainty is explicitly modelled, credits can be evaluated like any other risk-bearing asset.

  • Cash flows can be forecast with defensible assumptions

  • Reversal risks can be priced into contracts

  • Long-term performance can be monitored, not assumed

This is the threshold requirement for institutional capital. Underwriting clarity.

Second, contract structures evolve.
Instead of spot purchases or short-term offtakes, the market moves toward:

  • Long-duration offtake agreements (10–20 years)

  • Forward contracts linked to future credit generation

  • Blended finance structures with layered risk tranches

This creates predictability on both sides - developers can invest in higher-quality projects with longer payback cycles; buyers can secure supply at known price bands.

Third, capital costs compress.
Today, carbon projects often carry high implicit risk premiums because outcomes are uncertain and verification is intermittent.

As systems mature:

  • Better data reduces perceived risk

  • Standardization improves comparability

  • Liquidity deepens secondary markets

The result is lower cost of capital, which directly translates into more viable projects and higher-quality supply.

Fourth, the market deepens beyond compliance and CSR budgets.
Once credits are credible financial instruments, they move out of sustainability silos and into core capital allocation decisions.

  • Infrastructure funds can allocate to land-based carbon assets

  • Insurance capital can underwrite permanence risk

  • Sovereign and pension capital can enter through structured products

At that point, the market starts to resemble a new asset class anchored in real-world biological and industrial systems.

India: The Real Stress Test

India is where that question gets real. Fragmented smallholders, policy overlays, uneven data, and the need to aggregate execution at scale make it the hardest place to build this market and the most revealing one. If carbon markets can be designed to work here, they can survive real-world complexity anywhere.

Building Carbon Markets in India

India is not a clean test environment. It is fragmented, policy-heavy, and operationally complex. That is precisely why success here matters.

A functional carbon market in India will not look like a simplified Western model scaled up. It will be built around constraints and will derive its strength from handling them.

1. Aggregation at Scale, Without Losing Fidelity

India’s carbon market will be built on smallholders.

  • FPOs (Farmer Producer Organizations) and cooperatives acting as primary aggregation layers

  • Standardized digital interfaces for farmer data capture

  • Geo-tagged, time-stamped activity records integrated into MRV systems

The challenge is preserving granularity at scale.

2. MRV Built on Digital Public Infrastructure

India already has the rails:

  • Satellite data (ISRO) for land-use and crop monitoring

  • Weather and soil datasets for baseline calibration

  • Aadhaar-linked systems for identity and payments

MRV becomes a data infrastructure problem, not a project-level workaround.

  • Continuous monitoring replaces periodic verification

  • Data flows are automated, not manually assembled

  • Audit trails are embedded at the point of data generation

This reduces both cost and manipulation risk, while increasing frequency and reliability of measurement.

3. Making Farmer Economics Work

For carbon markets to sustain in India, they must work economically at the last mile:

  • Direct Benefit Transfers (DBT) linked to verified outcomes

  • Clear revenue-sharing models between developers, aggregators, and farmers

  • Predictable payout timelines tied to credit issuance cycles

If value leakage persists, farmer participation will degrade over time.

4. Designing for Policy, Not Around It

India’s policy environment is dynamic. Subsidies, state programs, and regulatory shifts continuously reshape incentives.

A successful carbon market does not treat this as noise. It integrates it.

  • Additionality frameworks explicitly account for existing schemes (e.g., organic farming incentives, LPG distribution)

  • Baselines are periodically recalibrated to reflect policy-driven adoption

  • Projects are structured with buffers against regulatory shocks

This reduces the risk of sudden invalidation and improves long-term credibility.

5. Standardization Without Oversimplification

Given India’s diversity - across soil types, climates, and farming practices - over-standardization can be as damaging as fragmentation.

Success lies in bounded standardization:

  • Region-specific baseline libraries

  • Methodologies tailored to agro-climatic zones

  • Shared data layers with localized calibration

This allows comparability across projects without erasing underlying variability.

6. A Tiered Market Will Emerge

Not all credits will be equal. A mature Indian market will likely stratify into:

  • High-integrity, high-price credits (dense MRV, strong permanence)

  • Mid-tier credits with moderate verification intensity

  • Commodity credits with lower assurance and pricing

The key is transparency of what they’re purchasing, and pricing should reflect underlying risk.

7. Built for Global Capital

India’s carbon market cannot be inward-looking. It needs to plug into global demand while maintaining local integrity.

  • Alignment with international standards (Verra, Gold Standard), but with localized enhancements

  • Acceptance by global buyers with stringent audit requirements

  • Development of export-grade credits that command premium pricing

India does not win by being cheaper. It wins by being credible at scale.

What Success Actually Looks Like

Success is not the elimination of uncertainty; it’s the honest handling of it. Carbon markets will always operate under uncertainty - biological systems are inherently variable.

But a working system does a few things well:

  • It measures uncertainty and prices it transparently

  • It replaces periodic validation with continuous observation

  • It aligns incentives across developers, verifiers, and buyers

  • It integrates policy as a core variable, not an afterthought

In that state, carbon markets start behaving like infrastructure - predictable enough to finance, flexible enough to adapt, and robust enough to scale.

Part 1 established the trust gap. Part 2 establishes the condition for closing it: carbon markets must shift from narrative-driven offsets to investable climate infrastructure.

India is the most important proving ground because it compresses the sector’s hardest questions into one operating environment: fragmented supply, policy complexity, distributed execution, and the need for credible, repeatable measurement. If a market can be built to clear those hurdles here, it is more likely to earn institutional capital.

That is the real test: can the carbon credits market be structured well enough to deserve scale.

item.title: Carbon Credits' Data Crisis: Why Trust Broke and Demand Didn't.
item.description: Part 1 of 2: Measurement, baselines, and the breakdown of trust in carbon markets.
item.dc:creator: Manasvi Patel
item.content:encoded:
We all have trust issues with carbon credits. Fair enough. Most of them are earned.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

But the popular narrative that demand is fading and that corporates are quietly backing away is lazy analysis. Demand isn’t disappearing, it’s evolving.

What’s actually happening is more structural: buyers are still here, but they’ve stopped trusting what they’re buying.

The Myth of Fading Demand

Everyone loves a clean collapse story. Carbon markets make for an easy target: inflated claims, shaky projects, and a few high-profile blowups.

Corporate net-zero commitments are still climbing. Retirements haven’t fallen off a cliff; what has changed is buyer behaviour. MSCI’s 2025 State of Integrity report lays it bare: corporate net-zero pledges surged 227% while retirements dipped just 7%. Fastmarkets clocked 2025 retirements steady at 169 million tCO₂e. BloombergNEF projects global supply ballooning 20-35x by 2050, split between $50-150/t high-integrity and sub-$10/t commodity tiers. Carbon Direct notes 95% of 2025 CDR credits were nature-based.

But here's the arithmetic that matters: global net-zero demands ~6 GtCO₂e annual removals by 2050. Renewables and electrification cover ~30-50% of the needed reductions. The rest - 24% from agriculture, plus aviation (12% of transport CO₂), cement (8% of global emissions), and steel (7-9%), cannot be fully electrified or renewed away. Without credible carbon credits, the Net Zero 2050 targets don't add up.

Buyers understand this existential math. Procurement teams now diligence credits like derivatives trades: rejecting anything without forensic-grade defensibility. The result is a barbell market: AAA-rated credits clear at 4x premiums, everything else struggles for bids.

The Mechanics (and the Illusion of Precision) of Carbon Credits

At a basic level, a carbon credit represents one tonne of CO₂ equivalent - either avoided or removed.

  • Avoidance credits: solar displacing coal, cleaner cookstoves reducing biomass use

  • Removal credits: soil carbon, forests, direct air capture

The system assumes you can measure, verify, and issue a tradable unit. This stack has a name: MRV - Measurement, Reporting, and Verification. The problem is step one.

The problem is step one. Carbon is not directly observable. It’s inferred using proxies such as satellite imagery, soil samples, activity data, and baseline assumptions. Each layer introduces uncertainty, and if you stack enough of them, you get something that looks precise, but isn’t.

Industrial projects operate within tighter bounds - grid emission factors, capacity utilisation, operational data - and you can get within a 10–20% error band.

Nature-based credits are the real plot twist.

Nature-Based Credits: High Potential, High Variance

This is where the system starts to break down.

Take regenerative agriculture in India. Farmers adopt no-till practices, cover cropping, and organic inputs. Soil carbon increases over time. Credits are issued based on the incremental gain over a baseline.

A slight digress – regen-agri is a set of farming practices designed to (in theory) turn farmlands into carbon sinks. Realistically, that sink is uneven, slow-moving, and incredibly sensitive to local conditions.

Soil carbon varies by:

  • Rainfall patterns

  • Crop cycles

  • Microclimates

  • Soil composition

Measuring it requires:

  • Multiple soil samples per hectare

  • Longitudinal tracking across seasons

  • Statistical modeling across fragmented plots

Now layer in India’s structure:

  • 85% smallholder farmers (<2 hectares)

  • Highly fragmented landholdings

  • Policy overlays (subsidies, state programs)

  • Monsoon-driven variability

A clean dataset doesn’t exist. What exists is a probabilistic system.

In 2025, these credits accounted for the majority of retired credits globally, with regen-agri prices jumping significantly. A Bayer pilot in Punjab certified credits from 10,000 rice farmers under the Gold Standard, boosting yields by 15% while cutting methane. Buyers love that story - it’s Scope 3 magic with a side of biodiversity brownie points.

So, What’s Actually Broken?

Strip away the noise, and the failure modes are clear.

  1. Measurement is indirect, but treated as definitive

    We are not directly measuring carbon; we are estimating it through a series of proxies and assumptions. These are inherently probabilistic, with each layer introducing uncertainty, and therefore the final output cannot be treated as a precise number.

    This creates a core mismatch: the system produces estimates, but the market consumes them as facts. That gap between probabilistic reality and deterministic issuance is where most downstream failures begin.

  2. Baselines can be negotiable
    Every credit relies on a counterfactual: what emissions would have been in the absence of the project. This baseline is constructed:

    • It depends on historical data, assumptions, and modelling choices

    • Small changes in assumptions can materially change credit volumes

    • There is no single “correct” baseline, only defensible ones

    When baselines become flexible, supply becomes elastic in the wrong direction. Credits CAN be created by adjusting the reference point rather than improving real-world outcomes.

  3. Incentives are misaligned
    The actors in the system are individually rational, but collectively misaligned. Each participant optimizes for their own objective function.

    • Developers optimize for maximum issuance

    • Registries optimize for market activity and throughput

    • Auditors optimize for repeat engagements

    • Buyers optimize for reputational defensibility

    None of these incentives are inherently wrong, but they do not naturally converge toward accuracy or integrity. Without structural alignment, the system drifts toward volume over quality.

  4. Verification costs do not scale cleanly
    High-integrity credits are data-intensive by design, and require consistent, multi-layered validation across time and geography.

    • Frequent sampling to capture variability

    • Cross-verification using multiple data sources

    • Long-term monitoring to ensure permanence

    This creates a cost structure that does not scale easily, especially in fragmented systems like smallholder agriculture. However, at the same time, the market continues to expect large volumes, competitive pricing, and rapid issuance cycles

    Something’s got to give, and usually, it’s rigour.

  5. Policy risk is ignored (until it isn’t)

    In markets like India, policy is an active force that shapes behaviour in real time.

    • Subsidies can eliminate the economic need for certain interventions

    • State programs can drive adoption independent of carbon incentives

    • Regulatory changes can alter project viability overnight

    Despite this, most carbon models treat policy as static or exogenous - it is neither.

    A cookstove project can be rendered irrelevant by free LPG distribution. A regenerative agriculture project can struggle to prove additionality if parallel government programs are already incentivizing the same practices.

    When policy is not explicitly modelled, it shows up later as broken assumptions.

    Taken together, these are systemic constraints. And until they are treated as such, the market will continue to produce outcomes that look coherent on paper but fail under scrutiny.

Taken together, these are systemic constraints, not isolated failures. Carbon markets are not a peripheral climate instrument; they are the only financing mechanism capable of mobilizing the removals and residual abatement and a net-zero target that otherwise collapses under its own arithmetic. That is why the market’s real challenge is not demand, but design. The architecture has to change.

The architecture needs aggregation models achieving execution density at low cost, hybrid MRV combining ground-truth geo-proofs with satellite signals to compress validation from 18-12 months, incentive structures making farmers economic stakeholders via transparent DBT payouts. Platforms that engineer farmer acquisition rather than announce MoUs, build audit-ready data from day zero, and model policy as dynamic input will separate credible supply from noise.

Countries with satellite infrastructure, digital rails, and vast degraded land hold the raw materials, but execution will determine who delivers the removals that the world cannot achieve without carbon markets.

Part 2: What it takes to turn carbon markets into climate infrastructure. The next frontier is not demand, it’s discipline. More Soon.

item.title: Rewiring the Grid: The System Behind the Energy Transition
item.description: The Indian power grid is the largest machine most of us will never see.
item.dc:creator: Transition VC
item.content:encoded:
The Indian power grid is the largest machine most of us will never see. It runs through forests and farmland, deserts and dense cities. It has been stitched together over decades of policy, engineering and political will. And over the next decade, it will either become the backbone of our energy transition - or the bottleneck that holds it back.

This is the system we are choosing to underwrite.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

The Evolution of India’s Grid

India today runs a single, synchronised national grid. Power that starts life as steam in a pithead coal plant or photons on a Rajasthan solar farm can be dispatched in real time to a data centre in Hyderabad or a pump set in a village in Bihar.

Generation capacity has grown in parallel, from roughly 305 GW to over 500 GW, with significant contributors being solar, wind, hydro and nuclear – in fact, in 2025–26 alone, India added over 50 GW of new capacity, around 80 percent of it from renewables. The ownership mix has also shifted, with private players now accounting for more than half of installed capacity, marking a transition from a state-dominated system to a more distributed supply base.

The Systemic Vulnerability of Distribution

While the transmission and generation sectors show clear progress, the distribution layer remains the most fragile link in the chain. State Distribution Companies (DISCOMs), despite supplying nearly 90% of India’s electricity, remain in deep financial distress.

Between 2015–16 and 2022–23, their accumulated losses rose by about 81% and debt by around 62%, reaching roughly ₹6.8 lakh crore and ₹6.6 lakh crore respectively.

A primary driver of this financial instability is the Aggregate Technical and Commercial (AT&C) loss.

Aggregate technical and commercial (AT&C) losses have fallen at the national level from about 25.5% in FY13 to 21.91% in FY21, and to around 15.4% in FY25, but they remain far above global benchmarks and exceed 30–40% in some states.

From an engineering standpoint, a portion of these losses is unavoidable. Technical losses typically range between 3–7% globally and arise from resistive heating in transmission lines, transformer inefficiencies, and physical phenomena such as corona discharge. The rest is commercial: electricity theft through illegal connections, unmetered agricultural supply, billing inaccuracies, and weak collection systems.

The Transition to a Data-Intensive System

For a hundred years, the grid was an electromechanical system: meters turned dials, linemen read them once a month, and then DISCOMs turned the readings into bills.

The grid is becoming a dense sensor network, and we’re moving from one reading per month to continuous telemetry, capturing not just volume, but voltage, power quality, and harmonic distortion across thousands of substations and feeders.

Instead of one reading per meter per month, discoms now collect 96 interval readings per day—15‑minute data streams that capture not just how much power a consumer used, but when, at what voltage, with what power quality, and how that behaviour aggregates across transformers, feeders and substations. Scaled to hundreds of millions of meters, this is a 3,000‑fold increase in data volume that pushes large utilities into the petabyte era.

This has several implications.

First, it means the grid is becoming a dense sensor network. Meter data can now, in principle, do far more than billing. It can:

  • Pinpoint where technical and commercial losses are actually occurring.

  • Monitor transformer and feeder loading in near real time.

  • Underwrite time‑of‑day tariffs and demand response programmes.

  • Help integrate rooftop solar, EV charging and other distributed resources without compromising stability.

Second, it means software—not just steel and copper—is becoming grid infrastructure. You cannot manually inspect petabytes. You need platforms that can ingest, clean and normalise data from heterogeneous head‑end systems, meter data management (MDM) stacks, billing engines and field operations tools, and then turn it into decisions: which transformers to replace this quarter, which consumer segments to prioritise, which pockets of loss will move the needle if addressed.

Third, it surfaces an uncomfortable truth: in most utilities, the software stack that sits on top of the grid was not designed for this world. As India scales to 250 million smart endpoints, DISCOMs are moving from a data desert to a data deluge. Collecting 15-minute interval readings (96 per day) represents a 3,000-fold increase in volume, pushing utilities into the petabyte era.

This final layer is where the energy transition moves from a “hardware story” to a “high-margin software story.”

The Emergence of the Orchestration Layer

To understand why the system is under stress, we must look at the current software architecture. Historically, utility software has been built in rigid, vertical layers:

  1. At the edge sits the Head-End System (HES), which communicates directly with meters and pulls in raw telemetry through RF mesh, cellular, or PLC networks.

  1. That data then flows into the Meter Data Management (MDM) system, which performs validation, estimation, and editing to ensure readings are usable.

  1. Finally, the data moves into customer information systems and billing platforms, where it is translated into revenue cycles, collections, and customer interactions.

The problem is not that these layers don’t work; it is that they do exactly what they were designed to do - move data reliably and produce bills, and nothing more. Each layer has its own database, schema, and vendor.

As a result, even basic operational questions require stitching together multiple systems; a utility manager trying to understand where losses have increased, or which transformers are driving the majority of outages, is often working across disconnected datasets.

Autonomy through the Agentic Layer

Once this layer is in place, the nature of the grid begins to change. The system moves from being observed to being managed, and decisions that previously required manual intervention begin to be handled automatically - this is the Agentic Layer.

  • Continuous Loss Identification: Instead of relying on monthly audits, AI agents compare energy flows across feeders and transformers in real time, identify discrepancies, and evaluate their likely causes (technical vs. commercial) before suggesting the next best action.

  • Predictive Asset Management: Instead of reacting to failures, the system monitors patterns of degradation across thousands of assets and recommends interventions before breakdowns occur, potentially extending transformer life by 2–3 years.

  • Higher-Level Interaction: Operators no longer need to navigate multiple reports. They can define outcomes at a high level—such as “reduce outages in Zone A”—and the agentic system decomposes that goal into a series of diagnostic and operational tasks across the stack.

Why is this the Investable Wedge

At this point in the stack, the source of value shifts from building infrastructure to operating it. India has already invested heavily in generation, transmission, and measurement, but the system still struggles to convert power into reliable revenue.

The constraint is no longer generation or capacity; it’s execution.

This is where the leverage sits. Even small improvements in loss reduction or collections translate into thousands of crores in recovered revenue at the system level. These gains are not abstract efficiency metrics, they determine whether DISCOMs can pay generators, service debt, and reinvest in the grid.

What makes this layer durable is how it integrates - it does not replace existing systems but sits on top of them, connecting fragmented data and turning it into operational decisions. As it becomes embedded in daily workflows, it compounds in value; the system learns the grid, optimises interventions, and becomes difficult to replace without disrupting operations.

The grid has been built, and this is the layer that determines its efficiency.

This is also where the market is structurally misbuilt today. The existing stack was designed for data movement, not decision-making. HES systems move data, MDM systems clean it, billing systems monetise it. None of them are designed to act on it. The result is a grid that is instrumented, but not intelligent.

Enter: WorkOnGrid.

WorkOnGrid operates as a unifying software layer across the utility stack. It ingests data from fragmented systems such as HES, MDM, billing and ERP, normalises it into a single data layer, and creates a continuous feedback loop between what is happening on the network and what actions need to be taken.

On top of this data foundation, it introduces a workflow layer that allows utilities to translate operational intent into execution. Instead of relying on static dashboards or manual audits, utilities can define outcomes, whether that is reducing losses in a feeder, improving billing efficiency, or managing asset health, and the system coordinates the underlying tasks required to achieve them.

This is complemented by a field operations layer that connects insight to action. Work orders, inspections, and maintenance cycles are not triggered manually but generated as a direct consequence of data signals, ensuring that operational decisions are carried through to the ground.

As this foundation matures, the system begins to operate with a higher degree of autonomy. The platform continuously monitors energy flows across the network, identifies discrepancies in near real time, and contextualises them using historical and operational data. It tracks asset health across thousands of transformers and flags high-risk assets before failure. It allows operators to interact with the system at a higher level, defining goals rather than executing tasks.

This is not theoretical. In live deployments, this approach has demonstrated the ability to isolate high-impact loss pockets, improve collection efficiency by 3–5%, and reduce AT&C losses by up to 2% points within months. At system scale, these are not marginal gains. They are the difference between a solvent and an insolvent grid.

What makes this layer particularly compelling is that it aligns with how the market is evolving. Smart meter deployments are scaling globally, data volumes are increasing exponentially, and policy frameworks are pushing utilities toward efficiency and accountability. At the same time, utilities do not have the ability or appetite to replace their core systems. The only viable path is a layer that can sit on top of existing infrastructure and make it work better.

WorkOnGrid is positioned as that layer.

It does not compete with the existing stack; it makes it usable. And as it becomes embedded across data, workflows, and operations, it moves from being a software product to becoming core infrastructure within the utility.

India has already built a 500 GW grid. Whether that system runs efficiently, recovers its revenue, and supports the next phase of the energy transition will depend on how it is operated.

item.title: Engineering the Carbon Economy
item.description: The Industrial Story Behind Our Investment in Intrinsic Foundries
item.dc:creator: Transition VC
item.content:encoded:
Today, we’re talking about carbon capture, more specifically, about how carbon capture evolves into industrial manufacturing.

The central question behind this investment was simple: Can carbon capture integrate into heavy industry in a way that strengthens business fundamentals rather than weakening them?

To answer that, we need to walk through: the structural gap in carbon capture, the biological lens to it, and how Intrinsic is addressing this.

Subscribe now

The Structural Gap in Carbon Capture

For the last several decades, the dominant carbon capture technology has been the amine system.

An amine system uses chemical solvents - typically amine-based liquids - that absorb CO₂ from flue gas streams. The flue gas is passed through a column where the solvent chemically binds to carbon dioxide. The solvent is then heated in a separate unit to release the CO₂ in concentrated form, after which the solvent is reused in a continuous cycle.

It works. The chemistry is well understood. Large-scale facilities have been built globally.

So why hasn’t adoption scaled? Because the economics create a structural gap.

In simple terms, installing an amine system means:

  • Spending large upfront capital - Capture costs typically range between $60–100 per tonne when regeneration and storage are included.

  • Consuming additional energy to run the system - power plants can lose 20–30% of output just to operate the capture unit.

  • Paying to compress, transport and store CO₂- Storing the CO₂ without generating new product revenue

As an industrial operator, this would mean higher capex and opex costs - without selling anything new. In other words, you spend money to remove something, and then you pay more money to bury it.

In markets with strong carbon compliance policies, that cost can be justified. In India, where cement and steel operate on thin margins and where there is no widespread CO₂ storage infrastructure, the financial incentive is weak.

That is the structural gap.

Carbon capture reduces emissions, but it does not improve the income statement. If that equation remains unchanged, adoption remains limited.

The Biological Lever in CCUS

So far, most carbon capture approaches have focused on physical, chemical separation and storage. The biological lever introduces a different idea: instead of separating CO₂ and burying it, convert it into something valuable.

Biologically, microalgae naturally fix carbon through photosynthesis, converting roughly 1.8–2x their weight in CO₂ into biomass. That biomass contains proteins, pigments, lipids, and specialty compounds that already have established markets.

Conceptually, this reframes carbon as feedstock.

However, previous biological approaches faced real-world constraints: industrial flue gas is not clean.

It fluctuates between 8–15% CO₂ and contains SOₓ, NOₓ, and particulates. Many algal strains optimized in laboratories struggled above 35°C, while industrial zones in India regularly reach 48–50°C. Productivity in earlier systems often stayed at 0.2–0.3 g/L/day, with capture efficiency around 40–60%. Photobioreactors made of borosilicate glass were capital-intensive and fragile, costing ₹20–30 lakh per kL

The biological pathway was promising, but the architecture was not built for industrial volatility.

Enter Intrinsic Foundries.

What Intrinsic Foundries did differently was design the system around industrial conditions.

They developed a carbon banking mechanism that buffers CO₂ as bicarbonate within the growth medium, storing up to 6 g/L equivalent per liter. When the flue gas supply dips, photosynthesis continues using stored carbon, and the capture efficiency remains in the 70–80% range.

They curated a non-GMO strain library tolerant to high CO₂ concentrations, impurities, and ambient heat up to 50°C.

They also redesigned the reactor manufacturing through on-site PMMA extrusion, reducing per-kL capex by roughly 60% at scale.

The shift is subtle but important: the system adapts to the factory, not the other way around.
